answers.text:
Transfer entropy is a specific information-theoretic measure used to detect directed, time-ordered influence between two signals — here, between two neurons' spiking activity. The article defines it a couple of sentences later: "Transfer entropy is well suited to measuring how much the past activity of one neuron (e.g., Xp) accounts for the immediate future activity of another neuron (e.g., Yt+1), conditioned on Y's own past (Yp)".

The key word is "conditioned." It isn't enough to know that neuron X's past predicts neuron Y's future — Y's own past already predicts its own future to some extent (its ongoing firing rhythm, refractory periods, etc.). Transfer entropy asks how much X's past adds beyond what Y's own history already tells you. The article makes the contrast with the other measure just introduced, mutual information: mutual information "does not, however, quantify information transfer between the neurons, as it is an undirected measure that describes the instantaneous dependency between two variables and has no notion of the time-directed structure that we intuitively understand as 'transfer' or 'flow.'" Transfer entropy fixes that by being directional and time-lagged.

This distinction is why the article later says "Whereas mutual information is a measure of functional connectivity, transfer entropy measures effective connectivity" — meaning it's used as a proxy for actual information flow along a connection, not just correlated activity. This sets up the rest of the section: the authors use transfer entropy first to map which neurons appear to send information to which others (building an "effective network"), and then, in the following sections, to select the source–target triads to which they apply the more elaborate partial information decomposition (PID) machinery that is the real subject of the paper.

Although not stated in this passage, transfer entropy was introduced by Thomas Schreiber in 2000 as a nonparametric way to detect directional coupling between time series without assuming a linear model, which is part of why it has become a standard tool in neuroscience for inferring effective connectivity from spike or field recordings.

answers.asked: Information-theoretic tools such as mutual information [10] and transfer entropy [11] are well suited to this purpose.
answers.text:
This sentence is naming the two specific measurement tools the article is about to unpack in the paragraphs right after it. It's a signpost, not yet the explanation itself — the actual definitions come next in the text (block spya-f6sbgx defines mutual information, and spya-p4pyuy defines transfer entropy).

The "purpose" referred to is stated in the sentence just before: given two elements, such as neurons, where one acts as an information source and another as a target receiving information from it, information theory's tools make it possible to track how neural activity propagates across a neural system. So both tools are being introduced as ways to trace how signals move from one neuron to another.

The bracketed numbers [10] and [11] are citations to the original papers that introduced each concept mathematically — mutual information traces back to classical information theory (Shannon's era), and transfer entropy is a later, more specialized measure built specifically for detecting directional, time-ordered influence between signals. The article itself draws exactly this distinction a few sentences later: mutual information tells you whether two neurons' activity is statistically dependent, but it does not... quantify information transfer between the neurons, as it is an undirected measure that describes the instantaneous dependency between two variables and has no notion of the time-directed structure that we intuitively understand as "transfer" or "flow". Transfer entropy is the tool built to fill that gap, since transfer entropy provides a measure of information propagation, capturing direction and timing that mutual information can't.

So this selected sentence is best read as a preview line: two named techniques are about to be defined, one for symmetric statistical dependence and one for directional flow, and the reader should expect the next two paragraphs to do exactly that.

answers.asked: What does "transfer entropy" mean here, and why does it matter to the argument?
answers.text:
Transfer entropy is defined in the article as a measure of how much the past activity of one neuron reduces uncertainty about the future activity of another neuron, over and above what the second neuron's own past already tells you [spya-p4pyuy]. As the glossary puts it, it captures how a source neuron's past activity cuts uncertainty about a target's future activity, after already accounting for the target's own history [spya-p4pyuy]. The article contrasts it with mutual information, which is undirected and simply measures shared dependence between two neurons without any sense of time or direction; transfer entropy instead measures "effective connectivity" — a directed, time-ordered notion of information flow — as opposed to mutual information's "functional connectivity" [spya-f6sbgx spya-p4pyuy].

Its role in the argument is mainly as scaffolding for everything that follows. The paper first tracks information flow with transfer entropy to build directed networks of "who talks to whom," and only then applies partial information decomposition (PID) on top of that structure to ask the deeper question of how information is processed rather than just transmitted [spya-qjdbvj spya-s0db2g spya-u5ra3d]. Concretely, the authors use transfer entropy to construct the effective networks from spiking recordings, identify triads (two source neurons feeding one target), and then decompose each triad's joint information into redundant, unique, and synergistic parts [spya-sw5ukx spya-tfcqnh]. Transfer entropy also turns out to be an empirical predictor of synergy itself: across 25 recordings, synergy was strongly correlated with the amount of transfer entropy in a triad, and was reliably about a quarter of that triad's transfer entropy [spya-kqkb58]. So transfer entropy is both the tool that builds the networks PID is applied to, and a variable whose relationship to synergy the article treats as evidence that feedforward information propagation predicts information processing [spya-kqkb58].

One caveat the article flags: because these networks were built from bivariate (pairwise) transfer entropy analyses, which are known to overestimate the significance of individual connections, this is one of the limitations noted for the in vitro findings [spya-j4cy9j].

In this abstract, "synergistic" labels one of the three modes the partial information decomposition (PID) framework splits information into — alongside redundant and unique. The passage tells you directly what it means here: it is information carried in the patterns of multiple inputs and is not reducible to input from any single source, and the abstract flags it as the mode the paper cares about most, describing it as the "higher-order" information a neuron extracts only by considering its inputs jointly.

The intuition, spelled out later in the article, is that if you add up how much each individual input tells you about a neuron's output, that sum can fall short of what you learn from looking at all the inputs together — the leftover, unexplainable-by-any-single-source portion is synergy. It's the signature of genuine computation rather than mere pass-through: a neuron isn't just relaying one input's signal, it's producing something new from the combination, e.g. detecting a specific joint pattern across two source neurons that neither alone would reveal.

The abstract also previews where this idea leads in the rest of the paper: synergy turns out not to be spread evenly through neural circuits but concentrated in particular places — network "rich clubs" (densely interconnected hub neurons), circuits with more feedback-loop-like ("recurrent") connections, and points where correlated activity streams converge — which the authors take as evidence about where and how neural computation is actually happening.

answers.asked: PID reveals redundant, unique, and synergistic modes by which neurons integrate information from multiple sources.
answers.text:
This sentence is naming the three outputs that partial information decomposition (PID) produces when applied to a neuron receiving signals from more than one source. It's the abstract's compressed preview of a framework the paper explains in full detail later, in section 4.

The idea is this: if you want to know how much a target neuron's future firing can be predicted from two "parent" neurons feeding into it, you can't just add up how predictive each parent is on its own — the combined predictive power isn't simply the sum of the parts. PID splits that combined information into three non-overlapping pieces. As the article later puts it, Red(X₁, X₂;Y) is the information about Y that could be learned by observing X₁ or X₂, Unq(Xᵢ;Y) is the information about Y that could only be learned by observing Xᵢ, and Syn(X₁, X₂;Y) is the information about Y that can only be learned by observing the joint states of X₁ and X₂ together.

In plain terms: redundant information is what either source tells you on its own (overlapping, "double-counted" knowledge); unique information is what only one particular source can tell you; and synergistic information is what only emerges when you look at both sources' patterns together — information invisible in either signal alone. The paper flags synergy as the one that matters most for "processing" in the computational sense, since if the system exhibits synergistic dynamics, the target neuron can be thought of as performing a kind of integrating "computation" on all of its inputs considered jointly, which is why the rest of the paper (the empirical sections on rich clubs, recurrent connections, and behaving primates) focuses so heavily on measuring synergy specifically, rather than treating all three modes as equally central.

answers.asked: What does "synergistic" mean here, and why does it matter to the argument?
answers.text:
"Synergistic" (or synergy) is the article's term for the piece of information about a target neuron's activity that is the information about Y that can only be learned by observing the joint states of X₁ and X₂ together — it isn't visible in either source neuron's activity on its own, only in the pattern of the two together [spya-h5jzvm]. The article introduces this via the joint mutual information equation, noting that the "whole" (information carried by both source neurons together) is not simply reducible to the sum of the "parts" (each neuron's individual information) [spya-h5jzvm spya-t02v4p]. When the whole exceeds the sum of the parts, that surplus is synergy: if the left-hand side of Equation (4) (the "whole") is greater than the right-hand side (the sum of the "parts"), then there is some information about Y that is disclosed by the joint state of all the neurons that is not disclosed by any individual parent. In this case, the system exhibits synergistic dynamics, and the target neuron can be thought of as performing a kind of integrating "computation" on all of its inputs considered jointly [spya-e94ury].

Why it matters to the paper's argument: the authors treat synergy as the actual signature of "processing" or "computation," as opposed to mere information transfer or passive relay. They say explicitly that plain information transfer measures only the "flow" of information but is limited in its ability to reveal how different streams of information "interact" and how neurons produce novel or modified information from multiple sources, which is why they turn to multivariate decomposition to get at processing itself [spya-s0db2g]. The whole empirical section of the review — synergy being enriched in "rich club" neurons, increasing with recurrent connectivity, and peaking with intermediate correlation among source neurons — is built on using synergy as the operational marker of where and when neurons are actually computing rather than just transmitting [spya-fud8q3 spya-sd9fzd spya-hkhpex]. The summary states this directly: We have focused particularly on statistical synergy, i.e., the information about the future of a target neuron that is disclosed by the higher-order patterns instantiated by multiple upstream neurons and is irreducible to any single source, as a measure of processing or computation. It goes on to argue that synergy's existence shows neurons do not appear to blindly sum the number of inputs and fire in response to the total (as would be expected from a basic threshold model or complex contagion model), but instead they are also sensitive to the particular patterns of incoming stimuli [spya-sp50v3]. So synergy is the concept that lets the authors claim neurons are doing something richer than passive summation — genuine pattern-sensitive integration — and it becomes the central quantity the whole review uses to connect network structure (rich clubs, recurrence) and behavior to "computation" in a measurable way.
